# Programming with Python {.unnumbered}

> *"Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for
> machines to execute."* — @abelson1996, preface to the first edition.

This part covers the first course of the master, **Programming with Python**.
It is aimed at people who want to learn how to design and build Python
programs that solve computational problems and manage data in real
applications. It starts from the role of programming, of algorithms and of the
development environment; it then teaches how to use variables and types to
acquire, transform and present information; how to organise related data in
collections and control the flow of a program with conditions and loops; how to
build reusable functions and model the world with classes and hierarchies of
objects. Once these foundations are in place, it shows how to handle errors at
run time, how to read, transform and save data in files, how to organise code
into modules and packages, how to use the standard library, and how to manage
dependencies in isolated, reproducible environments. It closes with the use of
AI tools to write and — above all — to *verify* code.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this course matters for an AI engineer
Every later part of the book (data analysis, machine learning, deep learning,
reinforcement learning, generative AI) is written in Python. Being able to
structure programs, handle data and manage dependencies is the technical
foundation that lets you move from a computational problem to organised,
working code.
:::

## Learning objectives of the course {.unnumbered}

At the end of this part you will be able to:

1. describe the role of Python and of algorithms in building software for
   different problems (@sec-ch-intro);
2. use variables, types and conversions to acquire, process and present data
   (@sec-ch-variables);
3. organise and manipulate related data with Python collections chosen
   according to their properties and access patterns (@sec-ch-collections);
4. implement program decisions by combining Boolean conditions and conditional
   branches (@sec-ch-conditionals);
5. implement iterations that process sequences and repeat operations until a
   termination condition holds (@sec-ch-loops);
6. design reusable functions that encapsulate operations and return
   consistent results (@sec-ch-functions);
7. build classes and hierarchies of objects that represent entities and
   behaviours through attributes and methods (@sec-ch-oop);
8. handle run-time errors by catching exceptions and defining appropriate
   checks (@sec-ch-exceptions);
9. read, transform and persist data through files and formats suited to their
   structure (@sec-ch-files);
10. organise code into reusable modules and packages, managing their
    dependencies and their public interface (@sec-ch-modules);
11. apply standard-library modules to common needs of system, time and
    calculation (@sec-ch-stdlib);
12. manage dependencies by choosing packages and controlling their
    installation, versions and distribution (@sec-ch-pip);
13. configure isolated, reproducible Python environments to run and share
    projects (@sec-ch-venv);
14. evaluate and verify code produced by AI tools, formulating adequate
    requirements and context (@sec-ch-ai-tools).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

None. You only need a computer with a web browser. Chapter
[-@sec-ch-intro] explains how to install Python or how to use it online.

## Map of the course {.unnumbered}

The table maps each module of the course (with its theory and practice
lessons) to the chapter of this book that covers it, and lists what the book
adds beyond the lectures.

| Module | Lessons (Theory / Practice) | Chapter | Additions in the book |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Introduction | course intro; computer programming; the development environment | @sec-ch-intro | von Neumann model, binary numbers (with proofs), algorithms and Euclid's algorithm, asymptotic notation, CPython and bytecode |
| 2. Variables and data types | input & output; variables & constants; data types; casting / I/O, types, casting, formatting | @sec-ch-variables | names vs objects, arbitrary-precision integers, two's complement, IEEE 754 floating point with error bounds, Unicode and UTF-8, format-spec mini-language |
| 3. Data collections | introduction to collections / lists; modify & check; nested lists; tuples; sets; dictionaries; length; casting between collections | @sec-ch-collections | dynamic arrays and amortised analysis, hash tables and their expected cost, sorting and its lower bound, aliasing and copies |
| 4. Conditional statements | Boolean expressions; logical operators; intro to conditionals / if; if-else; elif; the if expression | @sec-ch-conditionals | Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws, short-circuit evaluation, truthiness, `match` |
| 5. Loops | introduction to loops / while; for; break & continue | @sec-ch-loops | iteration protocol, loop invariants and termination proofs, binary search, comprehensions |
| 6. Procedural programming | introduction to functions / functions; positional & keyword arguments; return values; more examples | @sec-ch-functions | scope (LEGB), recursion and induction, the call stack, higher-order functions, type hints |
| 7. Object-oriented programming | classes & objects; inheritance & polymorphism / first class; special methods; docstrings; inheritance & polymorphism | @sec-ch-oop | the Python data model, MRO and C3 linearisation, Liskov substitution, dataclasses, abstract base classes |
| 8. Exceptions | introduction; anatomy of an exception; main exception types / try-except-finally; raise & assert | @sec-ch-exceptions | exception hierarchy, exception chaining, EAFP vs LBYL, context managers |
| 9. Working with files | file types / text read & write; binary; CSV; TSV; JSON | @sec-ch-files | encodings, RFC 4180 and RFC 8259, `pathlib`, atomic writes |
| 10. Modularising code | introduction to modules / module; package; a (real) package | @sec-ch-modules | the import system, information hiding, `pyproject.toml` and wheels |
| 11. The standard library | introduction / `sys`; command-line arguments; `os`; `time`; `datetime`; `math` | @sec-ch-stdlib | Unix time, the Gregorian calendar, compensated summation, `argparse`, `pathlib` |
| 12. PyPI and pip | the Python Package Index / install & uninstall; versions & upgrades; export & import | @sec-ch-pip | version specifiers (PEP 440), semantic versioning, dependency resolution is NP-complete |
| 13. Virtual environments | virtual environments / create-use-remove; Jupyter; Python version; sharing; crash courses | @sec-ch-venv | how `venv` works (PEP 405), kernels, lock files; primers on NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib |
| 14. AI tools for coding | code generation with ChatGPT, Cursor, Copilot; vibe coding vs structured prompt engineering | @sec-ch-ai-tools | how LLMs generate code, sampling and temperature, the pass@k estimator, verification checklist |
| Project | Terminal contact-book prototype | @sec-ch-project-phonebook | requirement-to-chapter map, design, full walkthrough |

## The final project {.unnumbered}

The course ends with the **terminal phone-book prototype** for the (fictional)
software house *ContactEase Solutions*: an interactive console application,
designed with object-oriented principles, that adds, lists, edits, deletes and
searches contacts, saves them to a JSON file, and never crashes on wrong input.
@sec-ch-project-phonebook restates the brief, maps every requirement to the
chapters above, and walks through the implementation published in
[`Phone_Book_Python_OOP.ipynb`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-projects/blob/main/Phone_Book_Python_OOP.ipynb).
